title: Chef Deepak Mishra to Open Bungalow 147, a 130-Seat Indian Restaurant in a Heritage Williamstown Bank
excerpt: The former Langham Melbourne executive chef is bringing Odisha and Bengal cooking to an 1869 waterfront bank building in Melbourne's inner west this summer.
body:
• Bungalow 147 by the Bay opens this summer at 147 Nelson Place, Williamstown — a 130-seat Indian restaurant inside an 1869 heritage-listed former bank on the Hobsons Bay waterfront.
  • Chef Deepak Mishra, formerly executive chef at The Langham Melbourne and vice president of Bocuse d'Or Australia, is opening his own restaurant after close to 30 years in luxury hotel kitchens.
  • The menu centres on the food of Odisha and Bengal — two eastern Indian cuisines Mishra says remain underrepresented in Melbourne — cooked with Victorian produce and European technique.
  • Downstairs holds the restaurant, wine bar, courtyard and veranda; upstairs private dining and event rooms look across Hobsons Bay.

Melbourne's inner west is getting an Indian restaurant with an unusual address. Bungalow 147 by the Bay will open this summer at 147 Nelson Place in Williamstown, inside a heritage-listed 1869 bank building on the waterfront — 130 seats split between a ground-floor restaurant and wine bar and private dining and event spaces upstairs, all of it facing Hobsons Bay.

A hotel chef goes out on his own

The restaurant is chef Deepak Mishra's first of his own after close to three decades in luxury hotel kitchens, including The Hotel Windsor, Hotel Chadstone, Pan Pacific Melbourne and The Langham Melbourne, where he was executive chef. He opened Swissôtel Kolkata, led kitchens at the Oberoi Rajvilas in Jaipur and worked at Fairmont Dubai, and he serves as vice president of Bocuse d'Or Australia, coaching Team Australia. "After almost thirty years in luxury hotel kitchens, I wanted to create something of my own," Mishra told Beat Magazine. "Bungalow 147 brings together my European culinary expertise, my Indian heritage and the style of cooking I've developed at Avani."

Odisha and Bengal, via Williamstown

The menu leans on the regional cooking of Odisha and Bengal, built for sharing — snacks and smaller plates first, then substantial dishes, breads and desserts — with seasonal Victorian produce and native Australian ingredients worked through the eastern Indian flavours. It is a deliberate gap in Melbourne's Indian dining map, which runs deep on Punjabi and South Indian kitchens and thin on the east.

"Eastern India has some of the country's most extraordinary food, and it remains underrepresented in Melbourne. I'm excited to have the chance to bring those flavours to Bungalow 147 where everyone feels at home."

— Deepak Mishra, Chef, Bungalow 147 by the Bay

The room and the drinks

The building is part of an 1869 pair at 145–147 Nelson Place designed by Michael Egan and recorded as contributory to the Nelson Place heritage precinct. Interiors by Micaela Cancino of Studio Argil draw on Indian bungalow culture — lime-washed walls, aged timber, brass and soft drapery. Wine is a centrepiece rather than an afterthought: the list draws on boutique Victorian and Australian producers, shaped with Rohit Singh, the second-generation winemaker at Avani on the Mornington Peninsula, where Mishra is culinary director. Cocktails run on tea, citrus, tropical fruit, Indian spice and native botanicals, alongside a selected whisky list, Sitchu reported.

For Melbourne's Indian community, the practical details: Bungalow 147 by the Bay, 147 Nelson Place, Williamstown, opening in the Australian summer of 2026, with the upstairs rooms pitched at private dinners and larger celebrations. A fine-dining Indian kitchen run by one of the city's most credentialled hotel chefs, ten kilometres from the CBD, is a booking worth making early.
